findings.issue: Source: "Agamemnon was convulsed with pain"; candidate: "Agamemnon shuddered with pain". A shudder is weaker than being convulsed by a spear-wound through the arm.
findings.fix: When noble Coon, Antenor’s eldest son, saw this, his eyes were sore at the sight of his fallen brother. Unseen by Agamemnon, he got beside him, spear in hand, and wounded him in the middle of the arm below the elbow, so that the point of the spear went right through the arm. Agamemnon was convulsed with pain, but even so he did not leave off struggling and fighting. He grasped his spear, which flew swift as the wind, and sprang upon Coon. Coon was trying to drag off the body of his brother, his father’s son, by the foot, and was crying for help to all the bravest of his comrades. Agamemnon struck him with a bronze-shod spear and killed him as he dragged the dead body through the press of men under cover of his shield. Then, standing over the body of Iphidamas, he cut off Coon’s head. So the sons of Antenor met their fate at the hands of the son of Atreus and went down into the house of Hades.

findings.issue: The Eilithuiae simile is restructured ("A woman in labor is sent sharp pangs by the Eilithuiae... The pangs that struck the son of Atreus were as sharp as those"). Both halves survive, but the order is slightly awkward for a general reader.
Source: "even so thick were the heads of them that fell by the hand of Hector"; candidate: "the heads of the men who fell... lay thick". Sense kept; "lay thick" is a small shift from "were thick".
Source: "Neleus was angered by what he had both said and done"; candidate resolves the pronoun to "what Augeas had said and done". Context (Augeas took the horses) supports it, so acceptable.
